faqs.question: What is the primary engineering difference between Flash DC House and conventional AC solar?
faqs.answer: Conventional solar systems generate Direct Current (DC), invert it to 230V Alternating Current (AC) using a central inverter, and then consumer appliances convert it back to DC via internal rectifiers, wasting 15% to 22% of solar power as heat. The Flash DC House uses a native direct-current bus to feed DC brushless appliances straight from the battery with zero inverter conversion loss.

faqs.question: Can the Flash Power Wall integrate with standard 230V hybrid AC inverters?
faqs.answer: Yes. While Flash Solar champions direct DC microgrids for maximum efficiency, the Flash Power Wall operates on a standard 48V/51.2V DC low-voltage battery bus and seamlessly integrates with compatible pure sine-wave hybrid inverters for properties with existing AC wiring.

blogPosts.title: Direct-Current Microgrids vs Traditional AC Solar: A Thermodynamic Comparison
blogPosts.excerpt: Why inverting DC solar to AC and back to DC inside appliances introduces unacceptable thermal losses and how sub-60V DC architectures fix it.
blogPosts.content:
## The Inversion Tax
In conventional residential and commercial photovoltaic installations, solar panels produce direct-current (DC) power. This electricity is fed into a central inverter to produce 230V alternating current (AC). When this power reaches modern electronics—LED lighting, brushless DC motors, computing clusters, and battery chargers—it is rectified back into DC by internal power supplies.

Each conversion stage sheds energy as heat, creating an aggregate thermodynamic loss between 15% and 22%.

## Sub-60V Direct-Current Distribution
By establishing a centralized 48V/51.2V DC low-voltage bus directly from the solar array and the Flash Power Wall, power flows natively into end-loads. Conductor losses are managed via proper copper busbar cross-sections, and central inverter failure points are eliminated.

## Conclusion
For modern energy engineering, direct current is not a legacy concept—it is the optimal engineering pathway for high-density, mission-critical renewable power.
